power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Retinal biomarkers and dementia risk: A review of evidence across the 14 Lancet modifiable risk factors for dementia

text.text: As the only central nervous system tissue that can be directly imaged non invasively using widely available technology, the retina offers a uniquely accessible window into the brain.

Quantitative retinal measures can be derived at scale and have been associated with mechanistic processes in the brain and throughout the body, positioning retinal biomarkers as promising tools for dementia prevention and intervention research.

E vidence indicates that several retinal biomarkers can distinguish individuals with Alzheimer's disease (AD) from cognitively healthy controls; however, it remains unclear whether these markers reflect preclinical AD -specific pathology or broader profiles of dementia risk, particularly in the earliest stages of disease.

This review synthesises current evidence on retinal microvascular and neuronal morphological biomarkers and their associations with 14 modifiable dementia risk factors identified by the Lancet Commission on dementia .
Robust evidence indicates that retinal biomarkers are influenced by vascular and metabolic risks, specifically hypertension and diabetes.

However, associations with other modifiable risk factors, including social isolation, lower educational attainment, hearing loss, smoking, air pollution, and traumatic brain injury, are sparse or absent.

Critical research gaps persist regarding how, when, and for whom the retina reflects vascular and metabolic risk factors , and whether non-biological risk factors , such as social isolation and educational attainment, are better understood as independent or confounding variables than as direct biological determinants of retinal biomarkers .

Clarifying these associations is essential to establish retinal biomarkers as scalable, non -invasive indicators of dementia risk and to support their integration into targeted risk stratification, early detection, and preventive intervention studies.

Dementia is one of the most pressing global health challenges of the 21 st century, affecting upwards of 50 million people worldwide and causing over 1.6 million deaths per year. 1 The recent development of disease -modifying treatments for Alzheimer's disease (AD) , which accounts for approximately 60% of dementia cases , 2 alongside recent findings from the Lancet Commission on dementia that approximately 45% of all dementia cases could hypothetically be prevented or delayed by addressing 14 modifiable risk factors from across the lifecourse , 3 has led to a renewed impetus for research into biomarkers of AD and dementia risk in the earliest stages of the disease.

text.text: The r etina has emerged as a promising window into the central nervous system as it shares several similarities with the brain that make it an ideal location for biomarkers of brain disorders , especially neurodegenerative diseases. 4 The retina arises from the same embryological and developmental pathways as the rest of the central nervous system, and shares a number of anatomical and physiological similarities including types of neurotransmitters and a blood -retinal barrier which is analogous to the blood -brain barrier. 5, 6 Furthermore, the retina can be imaged non -invasively using widely available technologies which are well tolerated by the public and often already embedded in routine healthcare services .

text.text: Dementia is a category of cognitive disorders, of which AD is the most common .

The pathophysiology of AD is characterised by the accumulation of extracellular amyloid -β plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles comprised of hyperphosphorylated tau protein , though vascular dysfunction has also been implicated in AD. 13 Other common forms of dementia include vascular dementia (typically diagnosed after isch aemic or haemorrhagic brain injury and characterised by cerebrovascular pathology ) and dementia with Lewy bod ies (characterised by abnormal aggregations of alpha -synuclein in cortical and subcortical areas) ; mixed aetiology is also common. 13 Retinal biomarkers may reflect systemic vascular, metabolic, and lifestyle exposures , including many of the recognised modifiable risk factors for dementia.

text.text: It is, therefore, critical to understand the relationships between retinal biomarkers and modifiable risk factors for dementia to best understand how retinal biomarkers can contribute to research on AD or other dementias , including for clinical trials, population screening, and health policy.
Retinal biomarkers have shown potential for early AD and dementia screening but cannot be interpreted in isolation from the broader health context of the population.
Modifiable risk factors may account for up to 45% of global dementia cases, 3 yet most retinal biomarker studies have not systematically examined whether these biomarkers track these risk factors.

It is critical that we understand the relationship between retinal biomarkers and modifiable risk factors for dementia to understand which pathological processes retinal biomarkers may be reflecting, and therefore in which situations these biomarkers should be used.
The aim of this review is to map the existing evidence on common retinal biomarkers and the 14 modifiable risk factors for dementia identified by the Lancet Commission.
These 14 risk factors are mechanistically heterogenous .
Several, such as hypertension, diabetes, and obesity, act through vascular and metabolic pathways with clear biological plausibility for altering retinal structure.
Others, such as social isolation or educational attainment, are not expected to leave a direct biological signature in retinal tissue.

Because dementia risk assessment checklists combine biological and non-biological indicators, mapping evidence across all 14 factors is necessary to establish which risk factors retinal biomarkers plausibly reflect, and which should instead be treated as independent, complementary variables in composite risk assessment.
Understanding these relationships is crucial for the interpretation of retinal biomarkers and determining whether they add independent value beyond existing dementia risk assessment approaches.
Retinal n euronal biomarkers : The retina is comprised of ten layers that line the posterior wall of the eye. 14 Two layers are of particular interest to neuroscientists and clinician -researchers .

text.text: The first is the retinal nerve fibre layer (RNFL), comprising the axons of the retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) which meet at the optic disc to exit the eye and form the optic nerve .
The second is the gangl ion cell layer (GCL ), comprised largely of the somata of the RGCs .
This layer is sometimes combined with the distal dendritic layer, the inner plexiform layer (IPL) , as the ganglion cell -inner plexiform layer ( GC-IPL ).
These layers are most commonly measured at their thickest point: RNFL near the optic disc (peripapillary region) , and GCL near the macula.
Another combined measure, the ganglion cell complex (GCC), combines all three of the above layer s , encompassing the somata, dendrites, and axons of the RGCs.

Approximately 90% of retinal nerve fibres travel to the lateral geniculate nucleus to synapse on neurons that terminate in the primary visual cortex , while the remainder synapse with neurons in the pretectal area. 14 As the RGCs synapse directly with the brain, it is thought that pathology present elsewhere in the brain may also be reflected in the retina. 4 Although research in the area of AD and dementia has primarily focused on the retinal layers that contain RGCs, the outer retina , which contains photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelium cells, has been associated with cognition and brain atrophy in older people. 15, 16 Retinal neuronal layers are typically imaged using optical coherence tomography (OCT) .

text.text: For each topic, search terms related to retinal measures and imaging techniques plus the risk factor of interest was searched (see supplement) .
Only studies with adults (18 years or older) were included.
For topics where a systematic reviews and/or meta -analyses had been published, these were prioritised.
Studies of patients with non-dementia -related conditions that affect the retina (e.g., Susac syndrome, glaucoma) were not included in this review.
In total, this review included 20 systematic reviews (including 16 meta -analyses) , 13 narrative or scoping reviews, and 10 original research articles.
Numerous lifestyle and psychosocial factors are known risk factors for dementia in later life .

The Lancet Dementia Commission recognise s 14 modifiable risk factors from across the lifecourse for dementia that together convey approximately 45% of dementia risk: education level, hearing loss, high LDL cholesterol , depression, traumatic brain injury, physical inactivity , diabetes, smoking, hypertension, obesity, excessive alcohol, social isolation, air pollution, and visual loss. 3 Here, we outline the evidence on associations between retinal measurements and each recognised dementia risk factor.

text.text: Education : Altho ugh lower education al attainment is a well -known risk factor for AD and is often included as a control or covariate in statistical models investigating associations with retinal or cognitive measures, education is rarely examined alone as a correlate or predictor of retinal morphology.

In one study, greater years of education were associated with greater fractal dimensionality and narrower arteries , veins, and venules ; however, the deep learning algorithm reported in the same paper did not predict years of education from retinal fundus images , 20 suggesting that any biological differentiation by educational levels may be slight.

text.text: Hearing loss is a recognised risk factor for dementia, and dual sensory loss (both vision and hearing loss) appears to convey increased risk for dementia and AD. 21 S everal conditions can be characterised by hearing impairments and involve retin al abnormalities , including Usher syndrome and Susac syndrome. 22 However, there is little research on whether hearing loss is associated with retinal changes preceding dementia outside of these syndromes , although microvascular retinopathy has been associated with hearing loss in two population -based cohorts. 23, 24 Hypertension : Narrowing of the retinal arterioles is considered a marker of systemic microvascular damage and chronic hypertension , and hypertensive retinopathy is characterised by microvascular abnormalities such as arteriovenous nicking, haemorrhages , hard exudates, and optic disc swelling. 25, 26 Elevated systemic blood pressure has been associated with narrower arteriole calibres and reduced superficial vascular density , while mixed results have been found for venule calibre , deep vascular density , and foveal avascular zone. 26, 27 S ystemic hypertension may be associated with high intraocular pressure, which in turn can result in RNFL and GCL thinning. 28 Evidence on hypertension and retinal neuronal layer thickness is evolving, with recent studies supporting an association between hypertension and RNFL and GCL thinning , particularly with longer duration of hypertension. 29, 30 Obesity : Obesity has been associated with wider venule calibre and reduced deep vascular density , though mixed results have been found for other microvascular measures such as arteriolar calibre and superficial vascular density. 26, 27 There are several hypothesised mechanisms by which obesity may influence the retina: chronic inflammation , oxidative stress , and impaired vascular autore gulation are all associated with obesity and can damage the microvasculature; obese individuals also typically have a higher total blood volume, potentially influencing microvessel density and calibre. 26, 27 Furthermore, comorbidities such as hypercholesteremia and hypertension may drive abnormalities in retinal microvasculature.

text.text: Less evidence exists for an association between obesity and retinal neuronal measures; a recent meta -analysis found weak associations between obesity and some RNFL measures. 31 High LDL cholesterol : Lipids perform essential functions in the retina and dyslipidaemia (an imbalance of lipids, including elevated LDL cholesterol) is a risk factor for a number of retinal diseases. 32 Although s everal papers that investigate associations between retinal measures and various metabolic measures include LDL cholesterol as a composite or covariate, few i solate LDL cholesterol as a specific driver of retinal alterations or look at the relationship outside of specific disease risks .

text.text: Several large cohort studies have found that high LDL cholesterol wa s associated with wider venular calibre, although no association was found with retinal arteriolar calibre. 27 A recent study found that older adults with higher LDL cholesterol had worse retinal microvascular measures than those with normal LDL, though no differences in RNFL , macular thickness, or FAZ measures across groups were found. 33 Depression : Because of the similarities between the retina and the brain, the retina has also been proposed as a biomarker for psychiatric disorders, including those that also convey increased risk for AD and/or dementia in later life such as depression .

text.text: Decreased r etinal thickness es , particularly RNFL, have been associated with depression in some studies, though evidence is mixed. [34] [35] [36] Some evidence suggests that r etinal microvascula ture and electrophysiological abnormalities may also be associated with major depressive disorder. 34, 36 Traumatic brain injury : TBI may predispose individuals to increased neurodegeneration, conferring increased risk for dementia, including AD and chronic traumatic encephalopathy. 37 E vidence suggests that retinal thinning can occur after TBI, even mild TBI, and this thinning may continue for years after injury. 38, 39 RNFL thinning has also been associated with worsening cognitive performance after TBI, as well as increased severity of TBI. 40 However, studies investigating the effects of TBI on the retina were scarce.

text.text: Physical inactivity : Physical activity acutely increases blood flow in the retina , and regular exercise may help mitigate age -related decrease s in macular and arteriolar blood flow. 41 In adults, physical inactivity is generally associated with narrower arterioles and wider venules ; further more , these measures may be modifiable through exercise interventions. 42 Less evidence exists for the effects of physical inactivity on retinal morphology outside of specific ocular diseases , although animal and mechanistic studies support a potential neuroprotective role of physical activity on retinal neurons and microvasculature. 41 Diabetes : The deleterious effects of hyperglycaemia on the retina have long been known , and diabetic retinopathy is a serious complication of diabetes mellitus that can lead to vision impairment and blindness , 32, 43 and is associated with increased risk for dementia. 44 Diabetic retinopathy primarily affects the retinal microvasculature, though diabetes also affects retinal neurons and glia , resulting in retinal thinning including in the RNFL and GCL. 43, 45 Tobacco smoking : Smoking is a risk factor for several ocular conditions including age -related macular degeneration and glaucoma ; 46 however, few studies have investigated the effects of smoking on retinal measures.

text.text: One study reported that greater childhood social isolation was associated with thinner RNFL in midlife, suggesting that retinal neuronal thickness might reflect long -term consequences of early social isolation. 52 In rats , social isolation resulted in thinner retinal layers after retinal hypoperfusion, implying that social isolation may hinder recovery after retinal injury. 53 However, the association between lifelong or late -life social isolation and retinal morphology remains understudied.

text.text: Air pollution : L ong -term exposure to fine particulate matter <2.5 µm (PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide ( NO2), and black carbon/PM 2.5 absorbance were associated with incident dementia , with insufficient evidence found for nitrogen oxide s (NOx ), fine particulate matter < 10 µm ( PM10), and annual ozone (O3). 54 There are few studies investigating the association between air pollution and the retina ; a recent scoping review identified only a handful of studies , in which long -term exposure to PM 2.5 and PM10 and acute exposure to black carbon were associated with decreased retinal arteriole calibre , while exposure to PM 2.5, PM10, and NO X may be associated with measures of retinal morphology. 55 Vision loss : Retinal tissue is essential for vision, and damage to the retina can result in visual impairment. 14 Three of the most prevalent retinal diseases (glaucoma, age -related macular degeneration (AMD) , and diabetic retinopathy) are among the leading causes of vision impairment and blindness, together affecting 19 million adults globally. 56 Vision loss was recently added to the Lancet Commission on Dementia's list of modifiable risk factors as a result of recent evidence that untreated vision loss is associated with an increased risk for dementia. 3 However, it appears that much of the association between vision loss and dementia may be driven by catarac t, which does not directly affect the retina , and diabetic retinopathy (discussed above). 57 There is some evidence that AMD is associated with increased risk for AD and dementia. 58, 59 Notably, AMD shares some pathological similarities with AD, such as amyloid -β peptides in drusen and similar neuroinflammatory responses, though whether these similarities represent shared disease mechanisms or reflect common age -related risk factors is n ot yet clear. 60 The link between glaucoma and dementia is less clear, with recent meta -analyses reaching different conclusions ; 57, 58, 61, 62 while methodolog ical heterogeneity among studies may explain the lack of consensus , it is possible th at shared risk factors for glaucoma and dementia such as age or cardiovascular risk may be obscuring associations.

text.text: While this review identified clear associations between retinal biomarkers and specific modifiable risk factors, notably hypertension and diabetes, empirical work exploring whether retinal biomarkers reflect the full range of modifiable risk factors remain s limited.

Very few studies that selectively evaluated education and social isolation as predictors of retinal biomarkers were found , and only a handful of studies were identified that investigat ed associations between retinal biomarkers and hearing loss, smoking, air pollution, and traumatic brain injury.

Dementia risk is increasingly understood through a prevention lens , where emphasis is placed on addressing modifiable risk factors ; 3 yet research on retinal biomarkers is frequently underpinned by an assumption that the retina reflects AD pathology, rather than a dementia risk profile that combines biologically -mediated indicators, such as vascular and metabolic dysfunction, with non -biological risk factors, such as psychosocial and behavioural exposures, that are not necessarily encoded in retinal tissue .
As focus shifts towards preventative interventions for AD and dementia, retinal biomarkers are ideally placed for research into interventions and policy.

A vital step in the translation al pathway is a thorough understanding of how retinal measures correlate with modifiable risk factors for dementia and how much of the biomarker signals reflect AD -specific pathology or earlier lifecourse exposures that contribute to dementia risk.

Retinal microvascular and neuronal biomarkers may reflect distinct biological risk profiles for dementia , potentially illuminating different biological pathways through which vascular and metabolic modifiable risk factors translate into dementia risk .

Retinal m icrovascular biomarkers reflect cerebral small vessel disease process es and vascular contributions to dementia, while neuronal biomarkers reflect neurodegeneration and axonal loss. 7 Substantive evidence s uggests that the retinal micr ovasculature is associated with a cardiometabolic risk profile that also includes hypertension, diabetes, and obesity, which implies that shared vascular pathways may be a mechanism linking these risk factors to dementia , support ing retinal microvascular biomarkers as a measure of cumulative dementia risk.

text.text: If further research establishes that retinal neuronal measures , such as RNFL and GCL , are more closely associated with AD -specific pathology than with modifiable risk factors, then they could be interpreted as biomarkers of primary neurodegenerative processes .
By contrast, psychosocial and behavioural risk factors, such as social isolation and lower educational attainment, are unlikely to alter retinal structure directly.

Any observed associations between these risk factors and retinal biomarkers more likely reflect shared upstream determinants, such as socioeconomic disadvantage or chronic stress physiology, or residual confounding, rather than a direct biological pathway from risk factor to retina.

These non-biological risk factors should therefore be treated as separate, complementary variables in composite dementia risk assessment, rather than as processes that retinal biomarkers themselves capture.
A critical issue in retinal biomarker research is a potential conflation between Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia.

The retina is comprised of both vascular tissue and neuronal tissue layers, and its anatomical and physiological similarities to the brain make it a feasible source of information on the pathological processes underway in the brain. 5 However, dementias are known for overlapping symptomology and misclassification , 63 and many studies of retinal biomarkers do not adequately distinguish biomarker -confirmed AD from other dementias, most notably vascular dementia.

text.text: Evidence suggests that retinal microvascular measures in particular may correlate with numerous domains of dementia risk , 64 suggesting that retinal microvascular biomarkers could be useful for capturing general dementia risk in settings where more specific risk assessment tools are not routinely used.

text.text: Retinal imaging has numerous benefits that make retinal biomarkers ideal for population -level use.

It builds on established infrastructure : most of the retinal biomarkers discussed in this review are derived from imaging modalities , such as fundus photography and OCT, that are already widely available in optometrists and ophthalmology departments, as well as in diabetic retinopathy screening programmes in many countries .
OCT and retinal fundus photography are noninvasive and well tolerated by the public .

The deve lopment of AI models to identify people with AD and dementia has demonstrated that retinal images have potential for scalable and cost -effective deployment. 65 Due to these benefits, retinal biomarker s could potential ly be used in numerous setting s , including enriching clinical trials for prevention or treatment interventions, population -based risk stratification screening , or precision -based medicine such as understanding effects of pharmaceutical treatments on the microvasculature to inform clinical decisions on treatment approaches. 26 Further research to understand the associations between retinal biomarkers and modifiable risk factors , as well as biomarker -confirmed preclinical AD, is needed to determine which biomarkers are suited to risk stratification, predictive, or prognostic uses.

text.text: Furthermore, the retinal microvasculature's insight into the cardiovascular system has led to researchers investigating the utility of retinal biomarkers for the diagnosis and monitoring of cardiovascular diseases as well as chronic kidney disease and diabetes. 66 Ensuring that retinal biomarkers accurately distinguish AD or dementia risk and are not simply reflecting a phenotype of cardiometabolic ris k is critical.

text.text: Thus, understanding the contribution of modifiable risk factors to each retinal biomarker is vitally important for translation, to ensure that screening programmes are appropriately calibrated, thresholds are validated, and predictive values are reliably estimated.

Increasingly, machine learning and deep learning models are being developed from retinal imaging, especially retinal fundus imaging; these are frequently trained to identify specific diseases (e.g., AD, chronic kidney disease ) and have shown some promise in distinguishing people with AD from healthy controls. 65 For these models to be useful, they must be able to identify people at risk for developing AD before they become symptomatic , and they should be able to do so in a population that will include people with comorbidities.

text.text: It is, therefore, crucial for the development of AI models to understand whether retinal biomarkers are a ssociated with risk factors for dementia.

Deep learning applied to retinal fundus images showed some accuracy in predicting 12 AD-related risk factors, including many of the risk factors included in this review. 20 Importantly, retinal biomarkers are likely to be most effective when combined with other dementia biomarkers, including fluid biomarkers such as p -Tau217, MRI imaging, tau -PET, amyloid -PET, or other biomarkers.

text.text: This requires the inclusion of retinal biomar kers in clinical trials and large cohort studies.

While some ageing focused cohort studies now include retinal biomarkers (e.g., UK Biobank, Dunedin Study, Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study), research on retinal biomarkers is still largely conducte d in studies of eye diseases.

A clear understanding of how retinal biomarkers could contribute to identifying individuals at increased risk for dementia requires data from population -based cohorts, including people with comorbidities.

Retinal biomarkers are indicative of risk for dementia, are associated with several of the vascular and metabolic modifiable risk factors that also drive dementia risk, and may be influenced by interventions that target these factors ; therefore, retinal biomarkers are promising candidate s to be included as a measure of brain health in studies.

The wide availability of retinal imaging technologies makes it ideal for use in population studies, while the development of portable OCT technologies may allow for retinal imaging in remote, resource -poor, and rural ar eas.

The development of machine learning models may allow for greater information to be extracted from retinal imaging, including risks for specific diseases as well as 'retinal ageing' derivative measures.
Retinal biomarkers may capture the cumulative imprint of biologically -mediated dementia risk, particularly vascular and metabolic exposures .

F uture studies must clarify how they relate to specific modifiable risk factors , including whether non -biological risk factors are better understood as independent complementary indictors rather than as processes directly reflected in retinal structure, and to the clustered patterns of risk exposure that unfold over the lifecourse.
